![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/45cfcf09b34366e9d63f61d9be13c0a5804151f5ad1e4411248002d06612281a.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=-\frac{4}{y}$ and $x=y+5$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{y} & =y+5 \\ -4 & ={y}^{2}+5y \\ {y}^{2}+5y+4 & =0 \\ (y+1)(y+4) & =0 \\ y & =-4,-1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=-4$ to $y=-1.$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/e559c357286114e2510a5e57016657ade81eb48439fe721f07c0e0380ae5e9d5.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=-\frac{4}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=y+5.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=y+5.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/fe0b5d26fd0ccbdb03646aa497226745db8f396e6e0be264691e329a118550e8.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-4}^{-1}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-4}^{-1}{[\,(y+5)-(-\frac{1}{2})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-4}^{-1}{[y+\frac{11}{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=-\frac{4}{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/0707f752a19e0dfcbe8defdaa600eeddd02ae98b8c9b35fee8fbf0480dd94be3.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-4}^{-1}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-4}^{-1}{[\,(-\frac{4}{y})-(-\frac{1}{2})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-4}^{-1}{[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{4}{y}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-4}^{-1}{[y+\frac{11}{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{-4}^{-1}{[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{4}{y}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-4}^{-1}({[y+\frac{11}{2}]}^{2}-{[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{4}{y}]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/67490fe1008a6c590389080456845a413928193ceced3248e924e476496b8f1b.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $y=\sqrt{x}$ and $y={x}^{3}$ for $x\in [0,1]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=2.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/846c6c56587f9f60aedf3952250c03f03e2a92ee90f067d1379ced74108b4296.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={x}^{3}.$

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={x}^{3}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/6c53fcb7d12f2aefb6e899c42441d048e93a43ce548812816b8882b76135f858.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(2)-({x}^{3})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-{x}^{3}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/0eab7ed4e195fa626db187071964bb14959678d5a04333d8760f5182ea93ed1d.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(2)-(\sqrt{x})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-\sqrt{x}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-{x}^{3}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-\sqrt{x}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}((2-{x}^{3})^{2}-(2-\sqrt{x})^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{6}-4{x}^{3}-x+4\sqrt{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(\frac{1}{7}\,{x}^{7}-{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{3}\,{x}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{1}{7}\,(1)^{7}-{1}^{4}-\frac{1}{2}\,(1)^{2}+\frac{8}{3}\,(1)^{3/2})-(0)] \\  & =\pi (\frac{55}{42}) \\  & =\frac{55\pi }{42}.\end{aligned}
$$

The region enclosed by the curves $x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+1$ and $x=y+1$ for $y\in [0,2]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-1.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/f61bbc9b42b775fbe10077320fe8a31ab905a4b45c8662d211310828fe9cb341.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+1,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=y+1.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=y+1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/c49c2b24b582be974f0e5148fc4898f3b3c39c9b1e6fcb450c496a099f29a4e4.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,(y+1)-(-1)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[y+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/17ce7b30d299a6bbef796e11da2589b9c26d760284d3915d472c7fe9103628a5.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+1)-(-1)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({[y+2]}^{2}-{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+2]}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(-\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}-{y}^{2}+4y)\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(-\frac{{y}^{5}}{20}-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+2{y}^{2})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi [(-\frac{{2}^{5}}{20}-\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}+2\cdot {2}^{2})-0] \\  & =\frac{56\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/c42ca982c8686217033bc529cdf5770c2f0e4300872c0a9dec80c04c0343ff2f.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x={y}^{2}$ and $(x+2)^{2}-7{y}^{2}=8$ for $x\ge 0$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=-2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
questions.worked_solution:
First, since we are rotating about a vertical line, we need to solve the equation of our second curve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{2}-7{y}^{2} & =8\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{7{y}^{2}+8}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we take the positive root since $x\ge 0.$

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =\sqrt{7{y}^{2}+8}-2 \\ {y}^{2}+2 & =\sqrt{7{y}^{2}+8} \\ ({y}^{2}+2)^{2} & =7{y}^{2}+8 \\ {y}^{4}+4{y}^{2}+4 & =7{y}^{2}+8 \\ {y}^{4}-3{y}^{2}-4 & =0 \\ ({y}^{2}-4)({y}^{2}+1) & =0 \\ (y-2)(y+2)({y}^{2}+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=-2$ to $y=2.$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/a28f7af71d91cccd233edd7bdbbf2f77ee531ccaf3ea277b53659fbfa3dc86a5.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x={y}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=\sqrt{7{y}^{2}+8}-2.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=\sqrt{7{y}^{2}+8}-2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/4eee8c5189271a201d1a3d303896234ce5b4195a6b128b6f41ace8ff91d2e2f3.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{[\,(\sqrt{7{y}^{2}+8}-2)-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{[\sqrt{7{y}^{2}+8}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x={y}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/1e7ee260c90acecc83ee186dc6f2acda5db4c841a2aa1a4516d3e1e414a976f9.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{[\,({y}^{2})-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{[{y}^{2}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{[\sqrt{7{y}^{2}+8}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{[{y}^{2}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}(7{y}^{2}+8-{({y}^{2}+2)}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

First, since we are rotating about a vertical line, we need to solve the equations of our curves for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-4)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =5\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{5-{y}^{2}}+4 \\ 3x+y & =17\,⟹\,x=\frac{17-y}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/f8baad5af3cd764cc1999527e60ad5cbe072b8ff7aee5f68925861c51ec7c65a.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{17-y}{3},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=\sqrt{5-{y}^{2}}+4.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=\sqrt{5-{y}^{2}}+4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/775a7a5109429b2ac547342932f96f66f490c6fb9f0d37a1d875aa041aa1eb8c.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\,(\sqrt{5-{y}^{2}}+4)-(4)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\sqrt{5-{y}^{2}}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{17-y}{3}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14268777/assets/57b54270d148d4cedf2c951f2407b77b898ef20f4238f4b3237c51bb70598df6.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\,(\frac{17-y}{3})-(4)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\frac{5-y}{3}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}({(\sqrt{5-{y}^{2}})}^{2}-{(\frac{5-y}{3})}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}(5-{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{9}(25-10y+{y}^{2}))\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{9}{\int }_{-1}^{2}(45-9{y}^{2}-25+10y-{y}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{9}{\int }_{-1}^{2}(20+10y-10{y}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{9}{(20y+5{y}^{2}-\frac{10{y}^{3}}{3})|}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{9}((20\cdot 2+5(2)^{2}-\frac{10(2)^{3}}{3})-(20\cdot (-1)+5(-1)^{2}-\frac{10(-1)^{3}}{3})) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{9}((40+20-\frac{80}{3})-(-20+5+\frac{10}{3})) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{9}(75-\frac{90}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{9}(45) \\  & =5\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

5.Computing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line?

The region enclosed by the curves (x−4)2+y2=5 and 3x+y=17 for y∈[−1,2] is rotated 2π radians about the line x=4. Find the volume of the resulting solid.
